title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 The Wrong Thing, Efficiently
author: Greg O'Keefe
summary: Greg O'Keefe synthesizes four decades of classroom observation research to name a persistent structural failure: the Cognitive Allocation Gap (CAG) -- the tendency of secondary schools to systematically over-invest instructional time in lower-order cognitive tasks while under-investing in higher-order thinking. John Goodlad's 1984 study of 1,000 classrooms found less than 1% of instructional time devoted to open reasoning; Larry Cuban's nine-thousand-record historical analysis spanning 1890-2010 showed that successive waves of reform changed almost nothing structural. Contemporary CASS data confirms that emotional support in classrooms has improved but instructional cognitive demand remains persistently low. Kathleen Cotton's questioning research (1989) established the still-valid 60/20/20 ratio: 60% of teacher questions are lower-order, 20% higher-order, 20% procedural. O'Keefe traces the mechanism to structural time pressure: higher-order questions require wait-time that 50-minute periods and coverage demands make structurally irrational. Theodore Sizer's 'Horace' is invoked -- a good teacher in a bad system making rational but educationally costly compromises. The CAG, O'Keefe argues, is not a pedagogical failure; it is a rational adaptation to structural constraint.
points: * John Goodlad's 1984 study of more than 1,000 American classrooms found that less than 1% of instructional time was devoted to discussions requiring open reasoning, student opinion, or inferential thinking -- a finding that remains statistically unchanged today. * The Cognitive Allocation Gap names the structural tendency of secondary schools to over-invest in recall and memorization while under-investing in the higher-order competencies research and the labor market identify as essential. * Cotton's 60/20/20 ratio -- 60% lower-order, 20% higher-order, 20% procedural teacher questions -- was established in 1989 and has remained stable or worsened; contemporary meta-analyses find lower-order questions at 70-80% in many contexts. * The mechanism is temporal: higher-order questions require extended wait-time with no ceiling effect on improvement, but coverage demands and 50-minute periods make that wait-time structurally irrational -- low-order questions are the rational adaptation. * Assessment data confirms the pattern: a 2025 analysis of a university entrance exam found 27% of items measuring recall, 50% measuring basic comprehension, and 23% measuring analysis -- with no items assessing evaluation or creation.
quotes: Less than one percent [of instructional time was] devoted to discussions requiring open reasoning, student opinion, or inferential thinking. -- John Goodlad, 1984
Cuban called it 'hugging the middle': teacher-directed instruction with student-centered gestures grafted on top. A hybrid that left the cognitive architecture of the classroom essentially intact.
The industrial default did not die. It acquired a better interface.
The 60/20/20 ratio is not a pedagogical failure. It is a rational adaptation to a structural constraint.

Horace is not a bad teacher. He is a good teacher operating inside a bad system. He knows his students would benefit from discussion, from argumentation, from sustained cognitive friction. He also knows he has 150 students, 50 minutes, and a curriculum to cover. -- Theodore Sizer
